hints: A path that starts with / starts from the top of the file system, not from where you are. Look at where full_path starts building every path, whatever the path begins with.

The likely mistake is thinking every path carries on from the working directory. A path that starts with / starts from the top of the file system, so the working directory shouldn't be part of the result at all.
solution_explanation: A path that starts with / is absolute: it starts from the top of the file system, not from where you are. So full_path drops the working directory's folders before following it. Relative paths still start from the working directory, with .. going up one folder and . staying put.
